articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow slides, S&P 500 wobbles as Nvidia clears hurdle, Anthropic prepares to price its IPO
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow slides, S&P 500 wobbles as Nvidia clears hurdle, Anthropic prepares to price its IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80.
The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday.
Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion.
The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range.
A representative for Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds.
Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.title_orig: Read Jim Cramer’s full interview with Nvidia’s Colette Kress: Demand, buybacks and China
articles.title_zh: Read Jim Cramer’s full interview with Nvidia’s Colette Kress: Demand, buybacks and China
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia delivered another beat-and-raise quarter on Tuesday in the chipmaker's first report since Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as CEO last week amid a widening affair scandal. Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, exceeding estimates by nearly $7 billion, while earnings topped expectations by 20 cents per share. An excellent quarter by almost any measure.
But investors remain skeptical about Nvidia's future without Huang, who famously founded the company at a San Jose Denny's in 1993. Shares fell 2.5% Wednesday, despite opening higher on the session. Will the company lose its smartest executives and engineers? Would Nvidia remain banker to the increasingly shaky neoclouds? Can it stay ahead of the competition?
On Tuesday night, Colette Kress sat down with CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after delivering her first earnings call as interim CEO to answer these pressing questions and more.
This transcript has been edited for clarity.
Jim Cramer: After the bell, Nvidia reported earnings, and what a quarter it was. The stock jumped in after hours in response. This is the first time we are hearing from the company since its founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as CEO last week. So let's check in with Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and now its interim CEO. Ms. Kress, welcome to "Mad Money."
Colette Kress: Thank you for having me, Jim. It's really great to see you.
Cramer: Thank you, Colette. The most important thing I heard tonight was that you increased your revenue growth forecast for next year. Previously, you said you would grow 70%. Now you're saying 75%, off of a higher base. How are you able to do that?
Kress: Thanks. Very, very important to understand how much our customers are interested in our compute infrastructure and how much they need the agentic solutions out there. So the most important thing that we have been seeing is just, again, a continuous growth in terms of the demand that's out there. But we also have been working in terms of our supply. So an increase in supply, working with all of our different suppliers, whether that be focusing in terms of what we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together. We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% year over year for fiscal year '28.
Cramer: Now, a lot of people have been saying that there was one man at this company. I've talked with you. There are another 49,000. How is the team holding up? Are there people who are saying, "You know what, this is not the Nvidia I know, I don't want to be there?" Is there a brain drain, as some people have told me?
Kress: Yeah, really great question. And remember, the company has been built on the perspective that employees see Nvidia as their life's work. And many of them have been here for decades, working with us from both a technology and a business-and-operations perspective. And now where we're standing is focusing on the business, focusing on getting all of that work done. And I had been working already with leadership. Leadership is supportive of everything we're doing and is standing up to help as we pull all employees and leaders together to move forward. But we have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy really the work here at Nvidia.
Cramer: I have talked to you many times about the idea that the cheapest stock in the world is yours, and that's why you don't necessarily have to help other people buy your chips when you can just go buy your own stock. Where are you on buybacks versus lending aggressive amounts of money to, say, neoclouds? Because I think that the buybacks are a lot better for shareholders.
Kress: We have now been looking at the capability of making significant stock repurchases for our company. That is enabled by our significant growth and the cash we will have. During the quarter, we discussed increasing the amount of additional stock repurchases to more than $150 billion. That adds to a total amount at this point of $277 billion that we're going to be able to provide. We are completely committed to that. We do believe that that's something we're going to be able to complete all the way through, just to the end of 2027. So we are in line and continuing our stock repurchases for sure.
Cramer: OK. Thank you. That's important. And it's more aggressive than I thought. And I'm glad to hear that. Now, why are there many different reports about your company, and even about your accounting? I know you as the person who is in charge of the numbers. For instance, I read two different analysts who say you may be on the hook for about $530 billion in guarantees, which is worrisome because it could have a huge impact on your cash flow.  I heard a new disclosure tonight that made me feel like the on-the-hook number is not true.
Kress: Right now, our guarantees have been thoughtfully completed to date. And our guarantees are approximately about $118 billion, which includes one of the most important ones: a land, power, and shell backstop that we have with Portsmouth here in the United States, the best site for what we see, the future of multiple, multiple buildings working together to do that, about 4.5 gigawatts to do so. That is solely for Nvidia's infrastructure. It's working very well and is getting ready for all the builds it needs to do. And that is the most significant part of our guarantees. We will continue to do the best due diligence and thought regarding any additional guarantees that need to be done. That means we're going to be working with companies to make sure we understand where they are in terms of their land, power, shell builds, how they are doing in terms of getting ready for the compute, getting the capital that they need, and making sure that they have the end customer, the off-take that we'll need to complete that. So it's going to be a top priority. But we are all working together to make sure that we can support the most important ones that we think are running very well, and that's going to be a top priority for us.
Cramer: Speaking of priorities, from a lot of reporting, again, because I want to try to get all this stuff out. You were kind enough to come on and speak about anything unrehearsed. Based on much of the reporting over the last two weeks, it seems that the aggressive investments in the ecosystem, including some companies that are less than investment-grade, were a priority for your predecessor and his family members. I want to know if you were pushing back on those? And should we see less and expect less support for the ecosystem and more for the shareholders?
Kress: Our investments are an important part of the work we can do, focusing on a set of organizations that may be AI-native, maybe new types of companies starting, as well as helping those that want to build new types of models in the market. These are some of the areas that we focused on. But, yes, we're very disciplined in terms of how we think that through. There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do. And we're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward. But most importantly, these are companies in areas where we can see additional growth in AI. And I think those are important for us. But, again, stepping back to our business and how important our capital is going to be for procuring supply and getting ready for all of our employees as well, and all the work that we need to do from the engineering, that's going to be our top priority in terms of our use of capital to do so. So that's what I think is the most important.

articles.title_orig: UnitedHealth and other insurance stocks drag down the Dow after CMS proposes new anti-fraud rule
articles.title_zh: UnitedHealth and other insurance stocks drag down the Dow after CMS proposes new anti-fraud rule
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Healthcare stocks fell again on Wednesday after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed a new rule that would toughen oversight of Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and the health insurance marketplace.
Sagging shares of managed care providers weighed on the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ), bringing the blue-chip index to a session low. UnitedHealth Group stock ( UNH ), one of the Dow's largest components with a 4.32% weighting, fell by about 8%. Humana ( HUM ) dropped 8%. Cigna ( CI ) shares declined by over 2%. CVS Health ( CVS ), which is in the process of splitting up its retail and insurance businesses, fell 3%.
Read more: Medicare out-of-pocket costs are rising in 2027
The rule, called the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, or CRUSH, would increase audits of insurance providers and allow CMS to recover improper payments. It would also require providers to report changes to enrollment information within 30 days, among other conditions.
In the release shared on Monday, officials pointed to bad actors billing Medicare for nonexistent wheelchairs, enrolling healthy seniors in Medicare-funded hospice care, and signing people up for Marketplace plans without their consent as examples of the kinds of fraud this rule aims to crack down on.
CMS said the rule could save taxpayers nearly $90 billion over the next 10 years. The proposal is open to public comment until Jan. 19, 2027.
However, Oppenheimer analysts said they expect the proposal to face similar legal scrutiny to that of a framework a federal court struck down in 2025. Furthermore, the team noted that the $90 billion cost savings likely reflect CMS recouping repayments rather than broad savings to healthcare programs.
"We believe CMS will be subject to the same legal challenges that it faced in 2025," the analysts wrote. "The substantially larger collection estimate reflects broader auditing, with recoveries concentrated in 2028–2030. This is a proposed rule, so CMS could choose to make adjustments in the final rule. Even if the rule were implemented as is, and it were upheld by the courts, we believe plans would incorporate the prospective cost into bids rather than absorb an unchanged recurring earnings burden."

articles.title_orig: Muslims to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, study finds
articles.title_zh: Muslims to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, study finds
articles.content_orig:
This Pew Research Center study tries to answer two broad questions:
We project future changes in the size and geographic distribution of seven religious groups – Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, Jews, followers of all other religions and religiously unaffiliated people – between 2020 and 2070. The projections cover 201 countries and territories, which collectively account for 99.98% of the world’s population.
The results are not intended to predict all the ways the world could change. There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics, and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analyzed here.
This research is part of the Pew-Templeton Global Religious Futures project , which analyzes religious change and its impact on societies around the world. It builds on our recently published work measuring the world’s recent religious makeup .
Many countries make demographic projections to try to forecast how their populations may change. The most common projection method – used by researchers for more than a century – starts by estimating the size of a country’s population in groups (“cohorts”) divided by age and sex, such as the number of girls ages 0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, etc. Each cohort is then projected into the future, modeling how its size will change every five years with the addition of expected births (based on fertility rates) and the subtraction of expected deaths (based on mortality rates). Demographers also often attempt to forecast future levels of immigration and emigration.
Our projections use an advanced version of this method. We pulled data from national censuses and surveys around the world to estimate the size and age distribution of each religious group in the baseline year, 2020. We incorporated data on differences in fertility rates between religious groups and on past patterns of movement into and out of each group, known as “religious switching.” Our projections also drew on data from the United Nations’ 2024 revision of its World Population Prospects, global migration flow estimates from University of Hong Kong professor Guy Abel, and the Center’s previous research on the religious composition of the world’s migrants . Read more in the methodology . Here is the complete list of sources used for each country and territory .
Our projection model was developed in collaboration with researchers in the Center for Advanced Studies of Population and Religion (CASPAR) at Krakow University of Economics.
You can explore the findings using our data explorer and sortable table . The custom software developed for these projections , which includes our input data, is available online.
For centuries, Christianity has been the world’s largest religion. That may soon change.
Muslims are expected to outnumber Christians by 2035, according to new projections from Pew Research Center. Both religious groups are growing in size, but Muslims are growing faster. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.
The world’s total population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070. Muslims and Christians are the only religious groups analyzed here that are expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.
As a result, the size of many religious groups will change relative to the world’s overall population. Muslims will make up a larger percentage of the global population in 2070 (36%) than they did in 2020 (26%). Christians, meanwhile, will hold fairly steady at 29%.
Although Hindus are growing in absolute number, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population. Jews are expected to follow a similar pattern. 1
Meanwhile, Buddhists are expected to shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population in the coming decades.
All other religions combined (including Baha’is, Daoists, Jains, Sikhs, adherents of folk religions and many other groups) are expected to experience a modest increase in number. However, they will slip below 2% of the global population by 2070. 2
And people who have no religious affiliation – sometimes called religious “nones” – are projected to drop substantially as a share of the world population, from 24% in 2020 to 17% in 2070. 3
Interested in projections for a specific religious group? Jump to sections of this study on: Christians | Muslims | Unaffiliated people | Hindus | Buddhists | Jews | Other religions
The future size of religious groups is heavily influenced by demographic trends in the countries and regions in which each group is concentrated .
In the 21st century, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly in countries south of the Sahara Desert. By 2070, more than a quarter of all people worldwide will live in sub-Saharan Africa . Since the vast majority of people who currently live there are either Christians or Muslims, the region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths.
By comparison, the populations of other major geographic regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even to shrink. For example, between 2020 and 2070, the number of people living in Europe will decline, and their share of the world’s population is projected to drop from 10% to 6%.
Fertility differences have big effects on populations. Globally, Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups. During the 2020-2025 period, the total fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman. 4 By comparison, the rate for non-Muslims was 2.0 children per woman.
The current age profile of the people in each religious group also plays a role in the projections. In younger populations, a larger share of people have yet to complete their childbearing years. On average, Muslims around the world are younger than any other religious group in this study. As of 2020, the median age of Muslims (24) was nearly a decade lower than the median age of non-Muslims (33).
If recent trends continue, by 2070:
These findings are part of a broader Pew Research Center project examining how the size of seven religious groups will change globally between 2020 and 2070 if recent demographic trends continue. Our projections take into account the differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration. (Religious switching and migration are assumed to continue at the same levels that have been recently observed.) We also incorporate mortality rates, applying the same rate to each religious group within a country. Read the methodology for more details about these projections and their limitations.
The rest of this analysis explores:
In the coming decades, religious groups will grow and contract at different speeds, reshaping the religious makeup of the world’s six major regions. Muslims are projected to grow as a percentage of the population in all six regions, while Christians will decline in all but one (the Asia-Pacific region). Still, Christians will continue to make up about half or more of the population in most regions.
If recent trends continue:
The United States is expected to follow roughly the same pattern of religious change as the overall North American region. 5 By 2070, Christians are expected to decline to less than half of the U.S. population, while religiously unaffiliated people will rise to about 41%. And Jews – who were the country’s third-largest religious group in 2020 – will be outnumbered by both Muslims and Hindus in 2070 if recent demographic trends continue.
The projected change among Christians and unaffiliated people will largely be driven by religious switching . Christians tend to lose more followers than they gain through switching in the U.S.

articles.title_zh: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
articles.content_orig:
Review scores for GTA 6 are a fairytale ending after years of development
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 , external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN , external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , external , but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times , external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
Critics say the relationship between Jason and Lucia is central to the game
The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian , external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes , external , Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post , external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg , external 's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (Â£760m).
GTA 6 is the most hotly anticipated videogame ever
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.
It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.
The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.
The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.
Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.
There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."
It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.
Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

articles.title_orig: Three killed as Israel launches first ground push since ‘ceasefire’ began
articles.title_zh: Three killed as Israel launches first ground push since ‘ceasefire’ began
articles.content_orig:
Israeli forces killed three Palestinians during a new operation in central Gaza on Wednesday, according to hospital officials, in the first broad ground offensive since a “ceasefire” was signed more than a year ago.
Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground reported that Israeli tanks were operating near Salah al-Din Street, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij camp.
An Israeli air strike targeted the town of al-Mughraqa, north of Nuseirat, killing one person and wounding several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera.
Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary said many Palestinians were fleeing areas in central Gaza as the Israeli operation got under way.
“We have been seeing people in eastern parts of Maghazi and Bureij, and people who are close to Salah al-Din starting to evacuate and flee the area due to the fact that there were huge explosions heard, live ammunition, and artillery shelling in that area,” Khoudary said.
“The Israeli forces in their announcement did not issue an evacuation order for people who are living in this area. They just mentioned that there is a military operation that is going to start, they are going to destroy the infrastructure and they are going to start demolishing in this area,” she added.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Israeli army said the operation aimed to “eliminate a threat” to its forces operating in the area of the “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the Israeli-occupied area of Gaza, and was established under the “ceasefire” agreement signed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025.
In a statement, the Israeli military said: “We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip.”
Hamas condemned the Israeli operation as a “flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”.
“Forced evacuation orders and the displacement of citizens carried out under the threat of violence and bombardment constitute a war crime and a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law,” the group said in a statement.
“The occupation’s actions are aimed at herding citizens into a narrow strip of the Gaza Strip, further exacerbating the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe,” it added.
Hamas said it holds Israel and the United States responsible for “the repercussions of the military operation and the crimes committed against civilians”.
Before the announcement of the Israeli operation, two Israeli drone attacks on Gaza killed at least two people, hospital officials told Al Jazeera.
Al-Shifa Hospital reported that one person was killed and others were wounded in an attack on the Sheikh Ijlin neighbourhood in southwestern Gaza City.
In a separate attack, Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital reported that one person was killed in Deir el-Balah in central Gaza, where the hospital had earlier reported an injury.
Earlier on Wednesday, Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that hospitals had recorded seven deaths and received 15 wounded people in the previous 24 hours.
Six people were killed by Israel over that period while one died from injuries caused by an earlier attack, the ministry said.

articles.content_orig:
Rayman Legends Retold , Ubisoft's upcoming remake of the ludicrously good Rayman Legends , has revealed another musical level, and it's wild.
We've had tunes in the past like Black Betty by Ram Jam and Eye of the Tiger by Survivor, but this new level goes for something a little bit more modern... A lot more modern, actually.
It's Dynamite by South Korean boyband BTS. Yeah, really!
Released in 2020 and later included in the album Be , it's the first song from the group to be recorded entirely in English. It went on to achieve enormous success, storming to the top of the Billboard Hot 100 chart and staying there for three weeks. Chances are you've probably heard it at some point, even if you haven't necessarily associated it with BTS.

Anyway, the level itself looks cool, if a little tame in terms of platforming. Hopefully it builds to a huge crescendo with come challenging moments, but we're definitely keen on the overall vibe and music. It's cool.
Raymen Legends Retold is scheduled to launch on 3rd December 2026 and will come bundled with Rayman Origins: Enhanced Edition .

articles.title_zh: Israel launches ground operation in central Gaza, dozens flee
articles.content_orig:
Israeli tanks advanced in an area of ​the central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, witnesses said, and the Israeli military said its forces were targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
The lates confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Dow slides 400 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides 400 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell on Wednesday as Nvidia shares lost momentum following the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings report.
The 30-stock index shed 459 points, or 0.9%. The S&P 500 traded down 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.3%.
Shares of Nvidia were more than 2% lower, reversing course from earlier gains after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
The report marked the chipmaker's first since Jensen Huang resigned last week as CEO, a move that came days after he admitted to an affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The company's board chair, Harvey Jones, said at the start of the earnings call that the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as chief executive.
"It's going to be an adjustment, but it's one that the market will work its way through, just as it always has in the past," said Eric Parnell, chief market strategist at Great Valley Advisor Group.
When it comes to the broader artificial intelligence trade, however, Parnell noted that the underlying fundamental challenges, including those related to capital expenditures and debt financing, haven't changed — and might not anytime soon.
"It doesn't take much of a slowdown in earnings growth in the environment that we're in with the AI buildout and the AI spend to take these types of stocks down pretty quickly," he said. "It's this type of volatility that I suspect we're not only going to continue to see but it's likely to increase as we go through 2027 and into 2028."
The Dow was also weighed down by losses in healthcare stocks like UnitedHealth as well as energy name Chevron and industrial giant Caterpillar . UnitedHealth lost 8%, while Chevron and Caterpillar declined more than 3% and nearly 2%, respectively.
On Tuesday, the blue-chip index dropped more than 1%, while the S&P 500 notched its lowest closing level since July 29. The Nasdaq shed almost 1% and touched its lowest level since April during the session.
Looking ahead, traders are awaiting the Federal Open Market Committee's minutes from its October meeting, which will also be out in the afternoon. Federal Reserve policymakers last month decided to keep the overnight funds rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
Investors are also looking ahead to a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic later this week. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Energy stocks fell alongside oil prices as investors reacted to last week's rise in U.S. crude and fuel inventories , even though tensions between the U.S. and Iran persist.
Shares of ExxonMobil and Chevron each dropped more than 3%, while others like ConocoPhillips and EOG Resources were down more than 2%.
S&P 500 energy was the worst performing sector during the session, falling nearly 3%.
That's as crude oil prices were lower on the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell more than 4% to $82.19 per barrel. International benchmark Brent crude futures slid more than 2% to $90.83 per barrel.
Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.
The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.
″[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Read more .
SpaceX shares are up more than 3% over the last five sessions as of late morning trading Wednesday, while the Nasdaq Composite is down more than 4%. That separation may be a sign of things to come, according to Morgan Stanley.
"As the AI trade diffuses into its next era, we see scope for further decorrelation and a more durable place in investor portfolios," analyst Adam Jonas wrote in a Tuesday note about SpaceX shares.
Two key things lead Jonas to this prediction: revenue from the company's connectivity — Starlink — vertical, the increasing need for SpaceX's Terafab as the U.S. seeks to create a more independent semiconductor supply chain.
However, a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, Elon Musk's other megacap company, creates a ceiling for the former's stock for now, he said. "Most investors we speak with are broadly comfortable with the merits of a potential combination," Jonas wrote, "but put off by the lack of certainty on timing and potential dilution risk."
Anthropic proxies gained ahead of the company's IPO. Here are some of the moves:
Shares of Amazon and Alphabet rallied 2% and nearly 1%, respectively. The two companies are direct proxies for Anthropic, given their independent investments in the AI company. In April, Amazon agreed to invest up to $25 billion in the company. That same month, Google said it plans to invest up to $40 billion in Anthropic , expanding on a longstanding partnership between the two companies.
Broadcom jumped almost 3%. The chipmaker is a major partner of Anthropic, having announced a special purpose vehicle to finance $63 billion in chips and networking products to be leased to Anthropic.
Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.
"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.
Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.
"That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC.
Read the full story here .
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Wednesday's session in the green.
The broad market index climbed 0.2% just after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq moved up 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 216 points, or 0.4%.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making moves before the bell.
— Davis Giangiulio and Fred Imbert
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation, which he said has been more persistent than he expected.
In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
From here, he said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.
"You might need to, like, shock people," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during the "Squawk Box" interview.
Read the full story below.
The recent crypto sell-off has led Citi to trim its targets for bitcoin and ether.
"We revise our base-case price targets for BTC and ETH to $99,532 and $2,838, respectively, as crypto's holding pattern has broken to the downside, with both assets down since our last update. BTC's break below its 200-day moving average prompts us to cut our near-term flow outlook to neutral," wrote strategist Alex Saunders. "ETF demand has deteriorated, with BTC flows slipping back into year-to-date net outflows and ETH recording outflows in each of the past seven weeks, while futures positioning points to deleveraging across tokens."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
articles.title_zh: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
articles.content_orig:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".
There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.
It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.

articles.title_orig: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
articles.title_zh: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.
“ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement . “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.”
The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.
This represents an important revelation from ULA and will provide some major relief to different parts of the US aerospace community, particularly Blue Origin and NASA.
That’s because the BE-4 engine is also the bedrock of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket. This powerful rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that was later attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
After this anomaly, Blue Origin retrofitted the main oxygen valve, including for Vulcan missions. Now it’s clear that this retrofit was not implicated in the Vulcan accident. With the preliminary Vulcan investigation having largely exonerated the BE-4 engine, Blue Origin can press ahead with its return-to-flight mission with New Glenn, which could occur as soon as January.
“Following the Vulcan anomaly, Blue Origin immediately worked alongside ULA to review flight data and support the investigation,” Blue Origin said in a statement Wednesday. “Together, we identified that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines. ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”
Amid a worsening US launch crunch, New Glenn offers the most tangible option for near-term relief for satellite operators, including Amazon Leo, which lost dozens of satellites on Sunday. The heavy-lift rocket has many commercial and government customers lined up for launch. NASA in particular is counting on the rocket to launch a number of lunar missions in the next two years, as well as play a significant role in landing humans on the Moon later this decade.
Also a relief to NASA will be confirmation that Vulcan’s upper stage, the Centaur V, did not contribute to the failure. NASA recently contracted with ULA to use the Centaur V as its new upper stage for the Space Launch System rocket, enabling future missions to the Moon.
For ULA, however, the latest update only brings more challenges.
Vulcan represents the company’s great hope to remain relevant in a US launch industry increasingly dominated by SpaceX and newer entrants such as Blue Origin. With Vulcan on the sidelines, other companies, such as Relativity Space, Rocket Lab, and Stoke Space, could also elbow out the once all-powerful launch firm.
Although Sunday’s Vulcan flight, its fifth overall, was the first outright mission failure for the rocket, two previous launches also experienced problems. Those issues involved the nozzle of the solid rocket boosters. ULA has now spent three years trying to move the rocket out of its teething phase and into regular operations. A successful launch on Sunday could have set up at least a monthly launch cadence next year.
Now, the cash-strapped company must also contend with a new issue involving propellant management and complicated plumbing that feeds liquid oxygen and methane to the BE-4 engines. It will certainly be offline for several months.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.title_zh: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump greets as China's President Xi Jinping welcomes him after Trump steps off Air Force One at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen in southern China's Guangdong Province, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, walks beside U.S. President Donald Trump during a welcome ceremony marking Trump's state visit to the Philippines at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Aaron Favila/AP hide caption
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at the APEC CEO summit held ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."
Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

articles.title_orig: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.
He was reciprocating the personal greeting he had received from Trump in September, when the American leader met him at the plane upon his arrival for a White House state visit . Lawmakers from both parties had criticized Trump over the move, which is also rare for U.S. presidents.
A report by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, said that during Trump’s arrival in the city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi noted the special trip the American president and first lady Melania Trump had made to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
“China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill,” the Xinhua report said.
After Trump descended from Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a quick hug as rows of military regiments and performers wearing bright pink and turquoise outfits stood at attention. A martial band played the American and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and Chinese and American flags.
Xi’s gesture Wednesday most likely reflects a desire by him and his government to “show respect to Trump,” which they know he enjoys, William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said in a post on X .
“It is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months,” he said.
When Trump last visited China in May, he was greeted at the airport in Beijing by Vice President Han Zheng.
Putin, who has a close relationship with Xi and has met with him 50 times as of Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader when he arrived earlier at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport. Putin was instead met by Cai Qi, a close Xi adviser and member of the Politburo Standing Committee.
Xi has met with a number of world leaders, including Putin, as they gather in Shenzhen this week for a summit of Asia-Pacific economies.
Trump, Putin and Xi are holding an unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.
Ahead of his bilateral meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected “great potential benefits” from the trilateral talks, which have sparked anxiety in places such as Ukraine, Iran and the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan, where officials worry the world’s three most powerful leaders could make decisions about their futures without consulting them.
In a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the trilateral meeting was unlikely to produce any sort of agreement, describing it as an “entry point” and “the first conversation.”
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.

articles.title_orig: Waymo suspends freeway driving after California construction zone complaint
articles.title_zh: Waymo suspends freeway driving after California construction zone complaint
articles.content_orig:
Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars’ driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times , this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.”
This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations.
In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.”
Waymo also told the government that the updated software is better able to respond to emergency vehicles when in a construction zone and that the company has made “operational changes that better identify and mitigate potential entry into pre-planned construction zones and enable more Remote Assistance capability” if it happens again.
Which it has. Despite the update to improve behavior around emergency vehicles, a video went viral in early November showing a Waymo robotaxi on I-280 driving past a pair of California Highway Patrol cars conducting a rolling roadblock as they held traffic behind a slow-moving construction vehicle. California also says there was an incident in which a Waymo robotaxi entered a construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame.
“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Waymo told Ars. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”
Waymo also told Ars it was continuing to work with the various California agencies that regulate transport.
Until the suspension, Waymo was only conducting highway operations in Los Angeles and the Bay Area in California, as well as in Arizona.
